title: Suffix Passives: ~이/히/리/기~
description: Convert active action verbs into their passive equivalents using specific single-syllable suffix extensions embedded directly into the verb root.
explanation: The Suffix Passive Shift

Unlike English, which forms passives using a helper verb ('to be seen'), Korean creates passive verbs by welding a single-syllable suffix—이, 히, 리, or 기—directly inside the verb root itself. This completely alters the sentence architecture: the original direct object shifts into becoming the primary grammatical subject.
The Suffix Sorting Blueprint
The specific suffix a verb accepts depends heavily on the final consonant sound of its stem root:
<ul>
• ~이~: Primarily targets vowel roots or stems ending in ㄱ, ㅂ, ㅈ (e.g., 보다 $\rightarrow$ 보이다 [to be seen], 놓다 $\rightarrow$ 놓이다 [to be placed]).
• ~히~: Targets stems ending in ㄱ, ㄷ, ㅂ sounds, frequently sparking an aspirated pronunciation change (e.g., 닫다 $\rightarrow$ 닫히다 [to be closed], 잡다 $\rightarrow$ 잡히다 [to be caught]).
• ~리~: Exclusively targets roots ending in the ㄹ batchim or verbs that trigger 'ㄷ' irregular mutations (e.g., 열다 $\rightarrow$ 열리다 [to be opened], 듣다 $\rightarrow$ 들리다 [to be heard]).
• ~기~: Typically attaches to stems ending in ㄴ, ㅁ, ㅅ, ㅈ sounds (e.g., 끊다 $\rightarrow$ 끊기다 [to be cut off], 안다 $\rightarrow$ 안기다 [to be hugged]).
The Agent Marker Change

In an active sentence, the person performing the action takes the subject marker (~이/가). In a suffix passive sentence, the external force or agent causing the action drops to a secondary role, taking the particle ~에게 or ~에 (e.g., 'by someone/something').
takeaway: Because these forms are deeply lexicalized, you must memorize which of the four suffixes pairs with each individual action verb.
cultural_notes: Passive formations are heavily favored in daily Korean speech when describing environmental occurrences or unexpected accidents where assigning explicit personal blame sounds too harsh or direct.
rules: Identify the terminal root sound of the active verb before running your suffix selection path.
Demote the original active subject agent by appending the ~에게 or ~에 particle to them.
Ensure the original object asset takes the primary ~이/가 subject marker in the passive frame.

examples.translated: The Namsan Tower is seen from afar. (Active 보다 becomes the passive 보이다).
The room door was closed because of the wind. (Active 닫다 takes 히 to become 닫히다).
The thief was caught by the police. (The police agent takes에게; 잡다 becomes 잡히다).
A mysterious singing voice is heard from outside. (듣다 undergoes a ㄷ mutation to take 리 $\rightarrow$ 들리다).

practice.prompt: Convert the active verb '열다' (to open) into its passive form 'to be opened'.
Convert the active verb '쓰다' (to write/use) into its passive form 'to be written'.
Convert '끊다' (to cut/disconnect) into its passive form 'to be cut off'.

title: Morphological Passives: ~어/아지다
description: Form passives for verbs that cannot accept the suffix extensions, or track an incremental transformation of state.
explanation: The Standard Passive Fallback

Not every active Korean verb can fit into the rigid $\sim$이/히/리/기$\sim$ suffix system. For verbs lacking a native suffix alternative—especially complex multi-syllable verbs or actions derived from Hanja (Chinese characters)—the grammar system utilizes the universal compound extension ~어/아지다.
Conjugation Integration Path
This structure attaches to action verbs using standard Present Conversational Inflection rules:
<ul>
• Bright Vowels (ㅏ, ㅗ): Attach ~아지다 (e.g., 찾다 $\rightarrow$ 찾아지다 [to be found]).
• Dark Vowels (어, 우, 이, etc.): Attach ~어지다 (e.g., 만들다 $\rightarrow$ 만들어지다 [to be made]).
• 하단 Verbs (하다): Shift uniformly into ~해지다 (e.g., 전하다 $\rightarrow$ 전해지다 [to be transmitted/passed down]).
The Adjective Mutation Split

You must stay alert to a major part-of-speech divergence. When ~어/아지다 attaches to an *action verb*, it serves a strictly **passive** function. However, when it attaches to an *adjective root*, it transforms that description into a process of change meaning **'to become...'** (e.g., 예쁘다 $\rightarrow$ 예뻐지다 [to become pretty]).
takeaway: Think of ~어/아지다 as the generalized, structural passive tool that steps in whenever a specific short suffix is unavailable.
cultural_notes: This grammar is widely preferred in journalistic writing and professional reports to maintain a highly objective, neutral tone (e.g., '이 사실은 널리 알려졌다' = 'This fact became widely known').
rules: Inflect the core action verb using regular 어/아 filters before cementing the 지다 framework.
Route any standard 하다 action base directly through the 해지다 conversion sequence.
Evaluate whether your base root is an action or adjective to clearly differentiate passive from change-of-state meanings.

examples.translated: This smartphone was made in Korea. (Action verb 만들다 combines with 어지다 in the past tense).
A legend-like story is being passed down in my hometown. (전하다 transforms into 전해지다).
Finally, the lost key was found. (찾다 leverages 찾아지다 to indicate passive discovery).
The weather is becoming warmer as time goes on. (Adjective 따뜻하다 uses 해지다 to mark an ongoing state mutation).

practice.prompt: Convert the action verb '이루다' (to achieve) into its passive form 'to be achieved'.
Convert '지우다' (to erase) into its passive form 'to be erased'.
Convert '깨다' (to break/smash) into its passive form 'to be broken'.

title: Suffix Causatives: ~이/히/리/기/우/구/추~
description: Infuse verbs with causative energy to show that the subject makes, causes, or allows an agent to perform an action.
explanation: The Causative Spark

Causative verbs indicate that the primary subject does not physically execute the action themselves; instead, **they manipulate, instruct, or allow an agent to perform it** (e.g., 'to make someone read' or 'to feed a child'). Like passives, morphological causatives embed single-syllable suffixes straight into the verb stem.
The Suffix Expansion Pack

The causative family features seven primary suffixes: 이, 히, 리, 기, 우, 구, 추. Because of this expanded list, many verbs have overlapping passive and causative forms that can only be identified through sentence context:
<ul>
• ~이~: Often binds to vowels or melting consonants (e.g., 녹다 $\rightarrow$ 녹이다 [to melt something], 먹다 $\rightarrow$ 먹이다 [to feed someone]).
• ~히~: Frequently tracks structural movements (e.g., 앉다 $\rightarrow$ 앉히다 [to seat someone], 입다 $\rightarrow$ 입히다 [to clothe someone]).
• ~리~: (e.g., 살다 $\rightarrow$ 살리다 [to save/revive], 알다 $\rightarrow$ 알리다 [to inform/make known]).
• ~기~: (e.g., 웃다 $\rightarrow$ 웃기다 [to make someone laugh], 숨다 $\rightarrow$ 숨기다 [to hide something]).
• ~우/구/추~: Target specialized native phonetic roots (e.g., 비다 $\rightarrow$ 비우다 [to empty], 솟다 $\rightarrow$ 솟구치다, 낮다 $\rightarrow$ 낮추다 [to lower]).
Particle Realignment

When building a causative clause around an active intransitive verb, the caused agent takes the object marker ~을/를. If the underlying verb was already transitive (holding its own object), the caused agent takes ~에게 or ~한테.
takeaway: Suffix causatives lean heavily toward immediate, direct physical causation (e.g., physically dressing a child vs. ordering them to dress).
cultural_notes: Using these verbs correctly is crucial for polite social dynamics when hosting guests, particularly when offering food or arranging seating locations (e.g., '여기 앉히세요' = 'Please seat them here').
rules: Identify the targeted agent and append the correct ~을/를 or ~에게 tracking marker.
Differentiate overlapping forms (like 알리다) by checking for an object noun elsewhere in the sentence.
Deploy these forms to emphasize a direct, hands-on causative action.

examples.translated: The mother feeds milk to the baby. (먹다 inflects via causative 이 $\rightarrow$ 먹이다 $\rightarrow$ 먹여요).

examples.kr: 친구는 나를 한 시간 동안 기다리게 하고 웃겼어요.
examples.translated: My friend made me laugh after making me wait for an hour. (웃다 takes 기 $\rightarrow$ 웃기다).
I seated the guest on the sofa. (앉다 takes the causative suffix 히 $\rightarrow$ 앉히다).
Please lower the radio volume a bit. (Adjective 낮다 utilizes 추 $\rightarrow$ 낮추다).

practice.prompt: Convert the active verb '죽다' (to die) into its causative derivative 'to kill'.
Convert '맡다' (to take charge of) into its causative derivative 'to entrust/assign'.
Convert the verb '깨다' (to wake up) into its causative derivative 'to wake someone else up'.

title: Syntactic Causatives: ~게 하다
description: Deploy the universal syntactic causative formula to express indirect causation, orders, permissions, or structural bypasses.
explanation: The Indirect Causative Option

When a verb cannot take a short morphological suffix, or when you want to express **indirect, non-physical causation** (like issuing a verbal command or giving permission), you use the universal formula ~게 하다.
Contrast of Direct vs. Indirect
Understanding the nuance gap between suffix causatives and ~게 하다 is a key hallmark of advanced proficiency:
<ul>
• Suffix Causative (Direct): The subject is directly, often physically involved in the execution (e.g., 어머니가 아이에게 옷을 입혔다 $\rightarrow$ The mother physically put the clothes onto the child).

• ~게 하다 (Indirect): The subject issues a verbal command or creates a situation that allows the action to happen (e.g., 어머니가 아이에게 옷을 입게 했다 $\rightarrow$ The mother told the child to put on their clothes).
Universal Structural Path

This grammar pattern is completely uniform. Suffix away the ~다 tail of any action verb or adjective root and append ~게 하다 directly, with zero exceptions for vowel or consonant structures (e.g., 공부하다 $\rightarrow$ 공부하게 하다).
takeaway: Use ~게 하다 anytime you want to highlight that you gave an order, granted permission, or influenced an outcome indirectly.
cultural_notes: In corporate settings, managers regularly employ this structure when delegating responsibilities to team members without sounding overbearing (e.g., '김 대리가 보고서를 작성하게 하세요' = 'Have Assistant Manager Kim prepare the report').
rules: Isolate the verb or adjective base stem cleanly without modifying its internal core components.
Append 게 하다 directly to the base, inserting a space boundary ahead of the 하다 block.
Select this form intentionally over a suffix option to emphasize indirect influence rather than physical manipulation.

examples.translated: The teacher makes the students speak only in Korean. (Indirect directive using 말하게 하다).

examples.kr: 부모님은 내가 늦게까지 게임을 하지 못하게 하셨다.
examples.translated: My parents did not allow me to play games until late. (Negative causative construction using 지 못하게 하다).
I let the child sleep in the room. (Indicates granting permission or arranging a scenario indirectly).
Please clean the room cleanly. (Adjective target highlighting an expected result environment).

practice.prompt: Convert '생각하다' (to think) into the syntactic causative form meaning 'to make someone think'.
Convert the verb '출발하다' (to depart) into the syntactic causative form 'to make/allow to depart'.
Form the causative phrase meaning 'made someone drink' using 마시다 in the ~게 하다 template (past tense polite, ended with 했어요).

title: Intentional Actions: ~으려던 참이다
description: Express that you were just at the absolute verge of executing a specific action right when an unexpected event or interruption occurred.
explanation: The Verge of Action

The advanced intentional framework ~으려던 참이다 captures perfect real-time timing. It declares: **'I was just about to do X at that exact moment'** (often followed by an explanation of how someone else's arrival or a phone call interrupted or anticipated your plan).
Anatomy of the Grammar

This compound is a sophisticated mix of the high-intermediate intention suffix ~(으)려고 하다, the retrospective past marker ~더~, and the dependent noun 참 (the exact point/verge of an event), capped by the identity link 이다.
The Consonant Layout Split
Look closely at the final consonant layout of your action verb stem:
<ul>
• Open Vowel Roots: Attach ~려던 참이다 directly to the stem (e.g., 전화하다 $\rightarrow$ 전화하려던 참이다).
• Consonant Floor Roots: Consonant-heavy bases receive the acoustic bridge ~으려던 참이다 (e.g., 먹다 $\rightarrow$ 먹으려던 참이다).
• The ᄅ Exception: Roots ending in a bottom ㄹ batchim reject the padding completely, taking the vowel path (e.g., 만들다 $\rightarrow$ 만들려던 참이다).
takeaway: This pattern is typically paired with conversational focus particles like 마침 (just/coincidentally) to highlight a striking coincidence in timing.
cultural_notes: This grammar is the ideal polite response when someone calls or texts you right as you were thinking of them, creating an instant sense of shared rapport and connection.
rules: Slide 려던 참이다 onto open vowel or ᄅ-batchim verb stems without adding extra padding.
Deploy the 으려던 safety layer for action verbs blocked by a bottom consonant floor.
Pair this structure with the adverb 마침 to maximize conversational emphasis on the striking timing.

examples.kr: 마침 지수 씨에게 전화를 하려던 참이었어요.
examples.translated: Coincidentally, I was just about to call Jisu at that exact moment. (Perfect synchronization of timing).
I packed my bag and was just about to head out. (나가다 takes 려던 참입니다).

examples.kr: 안 그래도 지금 저녁을 먹으려던 참이었어.
examples.translated: Even if you didn't mention it, I was just about to eat dinner right now anyway. (먹다 uses the 으려던 bridge).

examples.kr: 자료를 다 정리하고 컴퓨터를 끄려던 참이었어요.
examples.translated: I had organized all the data and was just about to turn off the computer.

practice.prompt: Convert '사다' (to buy) into the intention form meaning 'I was just about to buy it'.
Convert '씻다' (to wash) into the intention form 'I was just about to wash up'.
Form the phrase 'I was just about to start' using 시작하다 in this pattern (past polite conversational ending, ending in 참이었어요).
